summary: Sets out a Bill of Rights for people and organizations that appear in public directory listings. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1417. Note that the abstract recorded in some indexes does not match the title.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of fair rules for phone-book style directories, so people can trust how their names and details are listed and used.

subtitle: Rights for people listed in public directories

tldr.problem: Public directories held information about people with no safeguards for accuracy or privacy.
tldr.mechanism: The North American Directory Forum sets out seven user rights: not to be listed, to be informed when listed, to see your entry, to correct errors, to remove information, to have your privacy protected by law, and to have these rights fulfilled promptly.
tldr.outcome: Replaced by RFC 1417, this early standard formalized privacy expectations in networked directories.

today: RFC 1295 was replaced by RFC 1417 and is informational. It represents an early effort to establish privacy norms in electronic directories.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content: The North American Directory Forum created this Bill of Rights as a privacy and security policy for electronic directories built on international standards. The document applies to entries in public directories, not private ones. Users could choose to list information publicly, privately, or in both places.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you put your name in an electronic directory, here are the rights you should have.

sections.title: The Seven User Rights
sections.content: The seven rights are: (1) not to be listed at all, (2) to be told when your entry is created, (3) to read your own entry, (4) to fix information that is wrong, (5) to delete specific information you do not want shown, (6) to have your entry comply with privacy laws, and (7) to have all these things happen quickly.
sections.plainLanguage: You can say no to being listed, see what is written about you, fix mistakes, hide things you want private, and expect this to happen fast.

sections.title: Scope and Context
sections.content: The rights apply to public directory entries in X.500 directories connected by the North American Directory Forum. Other parts of the directory could be restricted, and users could opt to list information in private parts instead of public ones, or both. Security and privacy controls were expected to enforce these rights.
sections.plainLanguage: These rules apply to the part of the directory that anyone can see, not the private parts.

references.text: North American Directory Forum, "User Bill of Rights for entries and listings in the Public Directory", RFC 1295, January 1992.
